_file: Scenarios for the /workflows/logs/v2 execution-log CURSOR walk. See README.md in this folder for the upstream model — the stub only applies the window when `dateType=custom` is present, and every cursor page re-serves the reference row, because the live endpoint does both.
_windowNote: `dateType=custom` is REQUIRED for the server to apply fromDate/toDate at all; without it the endpoint serves its own ~30-day default. The stub models that, so a collector that stopped sending the switch would see the fixtures diverge instead of silently reading a default slice. Bounds are INCLUSIVE upstream; the half-open [fromDate,toDate) filter is applied locally on top.

empty-window.why: An empty window is the ONE result an incomplete walk can fake for free. If a genuinely empty window cannot be told apart from a failed read, every completeness claim downstream is worthless. Page 1 comes back with zero rows, which terminates the cursor immediately — the only case where `rows.length === 0` is a real terminal signal.

server-window-plus-local-filter.why: Both filters, working together, and the reason the local one is kept even though the server now really does window. The stub is INCLUSIVE on both bounds (as the live server is, proven to the millisecond), so the row at exactly `toDate` arrives over the wire and must be dropped LOCALLY by the half-open `[fromDate, toDate)` rule. The row at 999 is excluded by the SERVER. If the local filter were removed, `at-to` would be published; if the window were not sent, `before` would be too.

window-starting-at-epoch-zero.planBullet: Empty and short execution windows (epoch-zero lower bound)
window-starting-at-epoch-zero.why: fromDate:0 used to be a special case: the collector expanded every window by a millisecond at the lower bound to hedge against undocumented upstream boundary semantics, that expansion was clamped away at epoch 0, and the window was declared incomplete because a row at exactly t=0 could not be proven present. The semantics are measured now — BOTH bounds inclusive on `createdAt` — so there is nothing to hedge and nothing to clamp. Epoch 0 is an ordinary lower bound and the row sitting on it is retained.

cursor-walks-multiple-pages.planBullet: A history larger than one page
cursor-walks-multiple-pages.why: The core of the design, and the shape the old time-partition walk could never reach. 250 rows at a page size of 100 must be recovered by FOLLOWING THE CURSOR, and the union must be all 250 with nothing double-counted — even though every page after the first re-serves the previous page's last row. A collector that concatenated pages would report 253.

short-page-is-not-trusted-as-terminal.planBullet: A history larger than one page (termination proof)
short-page-is-not-trusted-as-terminal.why: THE LESSON OF THE ORIGINAL DEFECT, encoded as a scenario. 40 rows at a page size of 100 come back in ONE short page — and the walk still spends a second request to confirm the cursor is exhausted, rather than inferring it from the page being short. Inferring completeness from page length is exactly what read 37 of 433 rows and called it complete. The extra request is the difference between proven and assumed, and `pages: 2` here is that proof.

page-budget-exhausted.why: A walk that runs out of budget with the cursor still live has provably NOT seen the whole log, and must say so rather than publishing what it happened to reach. 250 rows at 50/page needs 6 pages; the budget allows 2.

multiple-event-type-streams.why: `eventType` is optional but NOT repeatable on the descriptor, so N requested event types cost N INDEPENDENT cursor walks drawing on one shared page budget. Each query carries exactly one eventType and the streams merge without cross-contaminating.

repeated-rows.why: Dedup must key on content, and an ID-LESS row must never be collapsed silently. The three identical `dup` rows collapse to one (their id is part of the hashed content). The two identical id-less rows are two DISTINCT rows inside one response, so both survive - collapsing them was a silent undercount with no warning at all - and the third id-less row differs in content and survives on its own. Any id-less row makes the count unprovable, which is what LOG_EVENT_ID_MISSING says. It ALSO pins a second, real consequence: the id-less rows sort last here, so the page ends on a row that cannot supply `referenceId` — the cursor cannot be advanced from it and the walk stops with LOG_CURSOR_UNUSABLE rather than re-requesting page 1 forever on a half-reference. That is why this scenario is incomplete: not because dedup failed, but because the log was provably not walked to the end.

numeric-and-string-ids-are-one-row.why: Upstream has returned an id as both 5 and '5'. Hashing them unnormalised made them two distinct payloads sharing one id, which is the exact shape of a genuine LOG_DUPLICATE_ID_CONFLICT - a phantom contradiction an auditor would have chased. Ids are normalised to strings before hashing, so this is ONE row and there is nothing to warn about.

conflicting-duplicate-ids.why: Two rows share an id but not a content hash, so one of them is a lie and the collector cannot tell which. BOTH are retained as evidence and the window is declared incomplete - silently keeping the first would turn a contradiction into a confident answer.

missing-timestamp-unsaturated.planBullet: Missing event timestamp in an unsaturated partition
missing-timestamp-unsaturated.why: The partition is terminal (3 rows < 20) so the walk itself is fine, yet one row's [fromDate, toDate) membership cannot be proven. Per plan line 427 the row is retained as evidence and the REQUESTED window is still incomplete. A short page must not be allowed to launder an unplaceable row.

corrupt-higher-priority-timestamp-field.planBullet: Missing event timestamp in an unsaturated partition (present-but-garbage sibling)
corrupt-higher-priority-timestamp-field.why: `startedExecutionAt` is PRESENT and unreadable while `createdAt` parses. The old fallback took createdAt and said nothing, so the result was indistinguishable from a queued row that legitimately has no start time - and the window's [fromDate, toDate) membership was asserted through a proxy for a field that exists and could not be read. That is much closer to 'no parseable time => incomplete' than to a normal fallback, so the corrupt field is named and the window is incomplete.

fractional-second-precision.planBullet: Missing event timestamp in an unsaturated partition (fractional-second grammar)
fractional-second-precision.why: The ISO grammar accepts 1-9 fractional digits and normalises them by right-padding to exactly 3, but every fixture until now used either no fraction or exactly 3 digits — the one width where padding and truncation are both no-ops. So `.1` (which must be 100ms, NOT 1ms) and `.123456` (which must truncate to 123ms, not overflow into seconds) were never exercised, and a padding rule of `fraction.slice(0,3)` or `Number('.'+fraction)*1000` would have survived every test in the suite while moving events by up to 99 milliseconds — enough to cross a partition boundary in a minPartitionMs=1 walk.

unordered-single-page-is-sorted.why: The emitted order and the required order must DISAGREE, or the sort is proven by a tautology - deleting `events.sort` entirely survived the whole suite. One unsaturated page emitted strictly descending is the smallest corpus where the result order can only come from the collector's own sort.

transient-500-is-retried.planBullet: Transient upstream failure on a log read
transient-500-is-retried.why: Wide windows on this endpoint intermittently answer HTTP 500 and then serve the IDENTICAL request cleanly moments later — measured as 500/500/200/200 across four back-to-back identical calls, consistent with an expensive cold query timing out and then hitting a warm cache. Retrying is part of the endpoint's real contract, not a workaround: a walk that abandoned the window on the first 500 would publish a partial audit for a workflow that is perfectly readable. The retry is bounded and narrow — 5xx only, never a 401/403/429, because those are a dead credential, a refusal, and the throttle the circuit breaker exists to latch on.
